name: Tamil

script.overview:
Tamil script (தமிழ் எழுத்து) is an **abugida** written left to right, descended from the ancient Brahmi script. It is the leanest of the Indian scripts: just **12 vowels** (உயிர் எழுத்து, 'life letters'), **18 consonants** (மெய் எழுத்து, 'body letters'), one special letter **ஃ** (ஆய்தம், *āytam*), plus a handful of borrowed **grantha** letters (ஜ ஷ ஸ ஹ க்ஷ ஸ்ரீ) for Sanskrit and English words. There is no headline, no aspirated letters and almost no stacked conjuncts.

Every consonant letter on its own carries an inherent short **a**: க = *ka*. To show a bare consonant with no vowel, Tamil puts a dot on top called the **புள்ளி** (*puḷḷi*): க் = *k*. Consonant clusters are simply written as dotted consonant + next letter, side by side: க்க (*kka*), ந்த (*nda*), ஸ்ரீ (*srī*).

To write a consonant with any other vowel, you add a **vowel sign** to it, producing an **உயிர்மெய்** (*uyirmey*, 'life-body') letter. 18 consonants × 12 vowels = 216 uyirmey letters, but you don't memorise them one by one: the signs for ā, i, ī, e, ē, ai, o, ō, au are regular (ா ி ீ ெ ே ை ொ ோ ௌ). Note that **ெ ே ை are written *before* the consonant** even though they are pronounced after it (கெ = *ke*, கை = *kai*), and ொ ோ ௌ wrap around it (கொ = *ko*). Only **u and ū** are irregular: the sign fuses with the consonant in several different shapes (கு, டு, சு, து, கூ, பூ…), which you learn as a small set of families.

The 18 consonants are traditionally arranged in three rows of six: **வல்லினம்** 'hard' (க ச ட த ப ற), **மெல்லினம்** 'soft' nasals (ங ஞ ண ந ம ன), each paired with the hard letter above it, and **இடையினம்** 'medium' (ய ர ல வ ழ ள). The hard letters are a key to pronunciation: one letter such as க can sound *k*, *g* or *h* depending on its position (see the pronunciation section).

Tamil also has its own digits (௦ ௧ ௨ ௩ …) and special signs for 10, 100 and 1000, but today everyday writing — prices, phone numbers, clocks — uses ordinary Western digits 0–9.

groups.title: Vowels (உயிர் எழுத்து)
groups.note: Twelve vowels: five short–long pairs (a/ā, i/ī, u/ū, e/ē, o/ō) plus the diphthongs ai and au. The full letter is used only at the start of a word; after a consonant you use the vowel sign shown. Length is meaningful: பல் pal 'tooth' vs பால் pāl 'milk'.

letters.sound: Short a, like the u in 'but' (never the a in 'cat').
letters.strokes: Start with the small left loop, then the large curve and the vertical on the right.
Write அ, then add the hooked tail at the bottom right.

letters.sound: Short i, as in 'bit' but a little tenser.
Short u, as in 'put'. At the end of a word it is often reduced to a relaxed, unrounded ɨ.
Short e, as in 'bet'. At the start of a word most speakers say 'ye': எலி = yeli.
letters.signExample: கெ (ke) — sign goes BEFORE the consonant

letters.sound: Long e, like 'a' in 'cafe' held longer (no y-glide at the end).
letters.signExample: கே (kē) — sign goes BEFORE the consonant

letters.sound: Diphthong like 'eye'. At the end of a word in speech it often becomes a short e or a: இலை → 'ile'.
letters.signExample: கை (kai) — sign goes BEFORE the consonant

letters.sound: Short o, as in Spanish 'no' but clipped. At the start of a word often said 'wo'.
Long o, as in 'go' but a pure vowel without the w-glide.
Diphthong like 'ow' in 'cow'. Rare; mostly in names and loanwords.

groups.title: Pulli and aytham (special marks)
groups.note: The pulli (dot) kills the inherent vowel, like the Hindi virama. The aytham ஃ is a unique letter counted on its own; today it is mostly used with ப to write the English 'f' sound.

letters.sound: Puḷḷi: a dot above a consonant removes its inherent a. க = ka, க் = k. Every word-final consonant and every first member of a cluster carries it.
letters.strokes: A single dot written last, above the letter.

letters.sound: Āytam: three dots in a triangle. In old words it is a light h/kh sound before க (எஃகு = ehku). In modern writing ஃப = f and ஃஜ = z in loanwords.
letters.strokes: Three dots: two below, one on top.

letters.sound: Modern spelling for English f: aytham + ப.

groups.title: Hard consonants — வல்லினம் (stops)
groups.note: Six stops. None of them is aspirated (no puff of air). Each has more than one pronunciation: voiceless at the start of a word and when doubled, voiced (and often softened) between vowels and after a nasal. ற never starts a word; ட never starts a native word.

letters.sound: k at the start (கண் kaṇ) and doubled (க்க kk); g or a soft h-like sound between vowels (மகன் magan); g after ங் (ங்க ng).
letters.strokes: A cross-like stroke: horizontal, then the loop through the middle.

letters.sound: Usually s at the start and between vowels (சரி sari, பசி pasi); ch when doubled (ச்ச cch) or after ட்/ற் ; j after ஞ் (ஞ்ச nj).
Retroflex: tongue tip curled back to the roof of the mouth. ṭ when doubled (ட்ட), ḍ (almost a flap) between vowels.
letters.strokes: One stroke: down, then right — like an L.

letters.sound: Dental: tongue tip touching the back of the upper teeth (softer than English t). t at the start and doubled; d (almost English 'th' in 'this') between vowels.
p at the start and doubled; b between vowels and after ம் (ம்ப mb).
letters.strokes: Like a U with the right side taller.

letters.sound: A tapped or lightly trilled r with the tongue a little further back than ர. In modern speech single ற ≈ ர, but doubled ற்ற sounds 'ttr' (or 'tt' in Chennai), and ன்ற sounds 'ndr'.

groups.title: Soft consonants — மெல்லினம் (nasals)
groups.note: Six nasals, one paired with each hard consonant: ங–க, ஞ–ச, ண–ட, ந–த, ம–ப, ன–ற. Inside a word a nasal is usually followed by its partner (ங்க, ஞ்ச, ண்ட, ந்த, ம்ப, ன்ற), and the partner is then voiced.

letters.sound: The ng in 'sing'. Almost only seen as ங் before க: ங்க = 'ng' as in 'finger'.
The ny in 'canyon'. Usually as ஞ் before ச: ஞ்ச = 'nj'.
Retroflex n: say n with the tongue tip curled back. Common in the middle and at the end of words.
Dental n, tongue against the teeth. Used at the start of words and before த (ந்த = 'nd').
English m. A word-final ம் is often just nasalisation of the vowel in speech (மரம் ≈ maraṃ).
Alveolar n, like English n. Sounds the same as ந to most ears; it is used in the middle and at the end of words, ந at the start.

groups.title: Medium consonants — இடையினம் (approximants)
groups.note: Six continuants, including the famous ழ (ḻ) and the retroflex ள (ḷ).

letters.sound: A single tap of the tongue, like the tt in American 'butter' or Spanish 'pero'.
A clear l with the tongue just behind the upper teeth (as in 'leaf', never the dark l of 'full').
Between English v and w; lips barely touch the teeth.
The 'Tamil zh': curl your tongue tip far back without touching anything and say an r-like glide — close to the American r in 'girl'. Never a 'z'.
letters.strokes: Start with the loop on the left, then the tall right side with its tail.

letters.sound: Retroflex l: say l with the tongue tip curled back to the roof of the mouth.

groups.title: Uyirmey: one consonant with all 12 vowels
groups.note: Every consonant combines with every vowel in the same way as க below. Learn this row and you can read 216 letters. Watch the signs that go before (ெ ே ை) and around (ொ ோ ௌ) the consonant. In the old, pre-1978 style you may still see ணா றா னா and ணை லை ளை னை written with special ligatures on signs and old books.

letters.sound: + ி: a loop attached to the top right.
+ ீ: the loop closed into a spiral.
Irregular: a hook down from the right (see the u/ū group).
Irregular: a hook with an extra loop.

groups.title: The irregular u and ū letters
groups.note: u and ū have no single sign; they attach in a few shape-families. (1) A downward hook/loop: கு டு மு ரு ழு ளு. (2) A separate small stroke to the right: சு பு யு வு. (3) A tail curling down-right: து நு ணு லு னு. Long ū usually adds a loop or the ூ sign: கூ டூ மூ ரூ / சூ பூ / தூ நூ.

letters.sound: Stroke family: ச + small hooked stroke.
Long ū, hook family with extra loop.
Long ū, hook family with extra loop.
Long ū, tail family with an extra loop (not the separate ூ sign).

groups.title: Grantha letters (borrowed sounds)
groups.note: Extra letters taken from the Grantha script to write Sanskrit and foreign sounds. They are fully part of modern Tamil spelling, especially in names and English loanwords, though purists sometimes replace them (ஜ → ச, ஸ → ச).

letters.sound: k + sh together; a conventional ligature in Sanskrit words.
'shree/sree': the honorific prefix, written as a single ligature.

groups.title: Common clusters (consonant + puḷḷi + consonant)
groups.note: Tamil does not stack letters: a cluster is just a dotted consonant followed by the next letter. Native words only allow doubled consonants, nasal + its partner stop, and a few others after ய் ர் ழ். These patterns also decide how the stop is pronounced.

letters.sound: 'ttr' in careful speech; plain 'tt' in casual Chennai speech.

groups.title: Tamil digits
groups.note: Tamil has its own digits and, traditionally, separate signs for 10, 100 and 1000 (the old system was not positional). Today you will see them on temple walls, calendars and old documents; everyday life uses Western digits.

where: Tamil Nadu and Puducherry (India), northern and eastern Sri Lanka, Singapore (official language), Malaysia, and a large worldwide diaspora
tagline: One of the world's oldest living classical languages — over 2,000 years of literature — and still the everyday voice of tens of millions, from Chennai street stalls to Kollywood films.
intro:
**Tamil** (தமிழ், *tamiḻ*) is a **Dravidian** language, unrelated to Hindi and the other Indo-Aryan languages of the north. Its closest relatives are Malayalam, Kannada and Telugu. Tamil has a continuous literary tradition reaching back more than two millennia (the Sangam poems), and it is an official language in India, Sri Lanka and Singapore.

Tamil grammar is **agglutinative**: words are built by gluing suffixes onto a root, one meaning per suffix — வீடு *vīḍu* 'house' → வீட்டுக்கு *vīṭṭukku* 'to the house' → வீட்டுக்குப் போனேன் *vīṭṭukku pōnēn* 'I went home'. Word order is **subject–object–verb**, there are no articles and no grammatical gender for things, but verbs agree with their subject in person, number and (for 'he/she/it') gender. Politeness is built in: **நீ** *nī* is intimate 'you', **நீங்க** *nīnga* is polite 'you'.

The most important thing to know is that Tamil is **diglossic**. The written, formal language (*sendamiḻ*, used in books, news and speeches) differs noticeably from **spoken Tamil** (*pēcchu tamiḻ*), which everyone uses in conversation, films and TV. Written இருக்கிறது *irukkiradu* 'there is' is spoken இருக்கு *irukku*; written வருகிறேன் *varugirēn* 'I'm coming' is spoken வர்றேன் *varrēn*. Speaking the written form in a shop sounds like reading a newspaper aloud.

This course teaches **standard spoken Tamil** (the general colloquial heard in Chennai and across Tamil Nadu media) for all phrases and dialogues, written in Tamil script the way Tamils write casual speech (in film subtitles and chat). Vocabulary is listed in its **standard spelling**; when the everyday spoken form differs, it is given in the note (e.g. *spoken: irukku*). The script section teaches you to read both.
romanizationNote: The romanization shows how words are **actually pronounced**, not letter-by-letter. Long vowels have a macron: *ā ī ū ē ō* (Tamil distinguishes short e/o from long ē/ō — கொடு *koḍu* 'give' vs கோடு *kōḍu* 'line'). Dots under letters mark **retroflex** sounds made with the tongue curled back: *ṭ ḍ ṇ ḷ*, and *ḻ* is the special ழ. Because one Tamil stop letter has several sounds, the romanization changes with it: க = *k* at the start of a word and when doubled, *g* between vowels and after a nasal (மகன் *magan*, தங்கம் *tangam*); ச = *s* at the start and between vowels (சரி *sari*, பசி *pasi*), *cch* when doubled, *j* after ஞ் (*nj*); ட த ப become *ḍ d b* between vowels and after nasals. ற்ற is written *tr* (காற்று *kātru*; Chennai speakers often say *kāttu*) and ன்ற is *ndr* (நன்றி *nandri*). Single ற and ன are written plain *r* and *n* except in the script and pronunciation sections where the contrast with ர/ந is being taught. *ng* is always the ng of 'finger', never of 'singer'. *t* and *d* are dental (tongue on the teeth) — never the English t. Note also that word-initial e/ē is usually pronounced *ye* and o/ō *wo* (எப்படி = 'yeppaḍi'), and a final *-u* is often a relaxed, unrounded vowel.

pronunciation.title: ழ (ḻ) — the famous 'Tamil zh'
pronunciation.body:
ழ is the sound Tamils are proudest of — it is in the name of the language itself, தமிழ் *tamiḻ*. It is a **retroflex approximant**: curl the tip of your tongue far back towards the top of your mouth, **don't let it touch anything**, and let the voice flow. The result sounds somewhere between an American r (as in 'girl') and an l. It is **not** a 'z' or 'zh' at all — the common English spelling 'zh' is just a convention.

Many native speakers in Chennai and Sri Lanka merge ழ with ள (ḷ) or even ல, so you will hear வாழைப்பழம் said 'vāḷaippaḷam'. That is fine in casual speech, but a correct ழ is admired, and you should at least recognise it.
tips: Say a long American 'rrr', then slide your tongue tip even further back and slightly widen it.
Keep the tongue tip off the roof of the mouth — if it touches, you are saying ள.
Practise தமிழ், then add vowels: ழா ழி ழு ழை.
If you can't make it yet, an American r is a better substitute than an l.

pronunciation.title: ல (l) vs ள (ḷ)
pronunciation.body:
Tamil has two l's. **ல** is a clean, light l with the tongue tip just behind the upper teeth — like the l in 'leaf', never the dark, hollow l of English 'full'. **ள** is **retroflex**: curl your tongue tip back and touch the hard palate, then say l. ள has a slightly 'thicker', darker sound, and it colours the vowel before it.

The difference changes meaning constantly, and ள is very common: it is in the plural suffix -கள் *-kaḷ*, in அவள் *avaḷ* 'she', and in பள்ளி *paḷḷi* 'school'.
tips: Hold a mirror: for ல you see the tongue tip near the teeth; for ள it disappears backwards.
Doubled ள்ள is easiest to feel — start there: பள்ளி, வெள்ளை.
ள never starts a word, so if you hear an l at the start, it's ல.

pronunciation.title: ர vs ற, and the clusters ற்ற and ன்ற
pronunciation.body:
**ர** (r) is a single quick tap, like the tt in American 'butter'. **ற** (ṟ) was historically a stronger, trilled r made slightly further back. In modern speech a single ற between vowels sounds almost the same as ர, but spelling keeps them apart and careful speakers still trill ற a little.

Where ற really matters is in clusters. **ற்ற** is pronounced *ttr* (or simply *tt* in colloquial Chennai speech): காற்று *kātru* / *kāttu* 'wind'. **ன்ற** is pronounced *ndr*: நன்றி *nandri* 'thank you', not 'nanri'. ற also never begins a word.
tips: Single ர: one light tap, never the English r with rounded lips.
For ற, let the tongue flutter once or twice — like a short Spanish rr.
Read ற்ற as 'ttr' and ன்ற as 'ndr' — that one rule fixes many words.

pronunciation.title: Three n's: ந, ன and ண
pronunciation.body:
Tamil writes three n-letters. **ந** (dental, tongue on the teeth) and **ன** (alveolar, like English n) sound almost identical to learners; the spelling rule is simple — ந at the start of a word and before த, ன elsewhere. So you don't need to hear a difference between them.

**ண** (ṇ) is different: it is **retroflex**, made with the tongue tip curled back, like ட and ள. Before it, the vowel takes on a slightly darker colour. It changes meaning: மணம் *maṇam* 'fragrance' vs மனம் *manam* 'mind'. Tamil also has ங (ng) and ஞ (ny), mostly seen in the clusters ங்க and ஞ்ச.
tips: Practise ண்ட and ண்ண first (அண்ணா, இரண்டு) — the following ட helps you curl the tongue.
At the end of a word, ண் still needs the curled tongue: கண் 'eye' is not 'kan'.
ஞா at the start of a word is often said 'nyā' or simply 'nā' (ஞாயிறு = nyāyiru).

pronunciation.title: One letter, several sounds: the voicing rules
pronunciation.body:
Tamil script has no separate letters for g, j, ḍ, d, b. Instead, the hard letters **க ச ட த ப** change their sound according to position — and the rules are very regular:

**1. Start of a word → voiceless**: கண் *kaṇ*, தலை *talai*, பல் *pal* (ச → *s*: சரி *sari*).
**2. Doubled → voiceless and held**: அக்கா *akkā*, பத்து *pattu*, அப்பா *appā*, பச்சை *pacchai*.
**3. Between vowels → voiced, often softened**: மகன் *magan*, அது *adu*, கோபம் *kōbam*, வீடு *vīḍu*, பசி *pasi* (ச → *s*). In fast speech க between vowels can sound like a soft *h* (மகன் ≈ 'mahan').
**4. After a nasal → voiced**: ங்க *ng*, ஞ்ச *nj*, ண்ட *ṇḍ*, ந்த *nd*, ம்ப *mb*.

Loanwords break the rules (பஸ் *bas* 'bus', காபி *kāpi* 'coffee'), and Grantha ஜ gives a clear j. But for native words, if you can see a letter's neighbours, you know its sound.
tips: Look at the letter before: a vowel → voice it; the same letter with a puḷḷi → keep it hard; a nasal → voice it.
No Tamil stop is aspirated: keep your hand in front of your mouth — no puff of air on k, t, p.
Doubling = holding the closure a beat longer, as in English 'book-keeper'.

pairs.note: single ட between vowels = ḍ; doubled = ṭṭ

pronunciation.title: Short and long vowels (a/ā, i/ī, u/ū)
pronunciation.body:
Vowel length in Tamil is phonemic: a long vowel is held roughly twice as long, and the difference makes a different word. English speakers tend to shorten long vowels in unstressed positions — but Tamil has no strong stress, so every long vowel keeps its length wherever it is.

Short *a* is a central vowel like the u in 'but'; long *ā* is the a in 'father'. Don't reduce short vowels to 'uh' either: each syllable gets its full, even weight.
tips: Clap the syllables: a long vowel takes two claps' worth of time.
Short a = 'u' of 'cup', not 'a' of 'cat'.
Tamil rhythm is even and syllable-timed — avoid English-style strong/weak syllables.

pronunciation.title: Short vs long e and o
pronunciation.body:
Unlike Hindi, Tamil has both **short e, o** and **long ē, ō**, and they distinguish words. Short e is like 'bet', short o like a clipped 'o' in Spanish 'no'. Long ē and ō are pure, held vowels — don't add the English glides ('ay', 'ow').

The script shows the difference clearly: ெ (e) vs ே (ē), ொ (o) vs ோ (ō). Note also that at the start of a word, e/ē are normally pronounced with a y-glide (எங்க = *yenga*) and o/ō with a w-glide (ஒண்ணு = *woṇṇu*).
tips: ே has an extra loop compared with ெ — the loop means 'long'.
Say ē as in 'café' but freeze your tongue: no y at the end.
Say ō as in 'go' but keep the lips still: no w at the end.

pronunciation.title: Double consonants (gemination)
pronunciation.body:
A doubled consonant (written with a puḷḷi on the first: க்க, ட்ட, ல்ல…) is held for an extra beat, like the 'k-k' in 'book-keeper' or 'bus stop'. Tamil is full of them, and single vs double often changes the meaning. Doubling also changes how stops sound: doubled stops are always voiceless (பாட்டு *pāṭṭu*), single ones between vowels are voiced (பாடு *pāḍu*).

Doubling also appears at word boundaries: the dative -க்கு, and the sandhi rule that doubles a stop after certain words: வீட்டுக்குப் போ *vīṭṭukkup pō* 'go home'.
tips: Pause on the closure: 'pat-tu', 'kaṭ-ṭai'.
Don't add a vowel between the two halves.
Doubled l, ḷ, n, ṇ, m are held too: அம்மா, நல்ல, வெள்ளை, அண்ணா.

pronunciation.title: Retroflex vs dental: ட/த, ண/ந, ள/ல
pronunciation.body:
Tamil contrasts **dental** sounds (tongue tip touching the back of the upper teeth: த ந ல) with **retroflex** sounds (tongue tip curled back to touch the roof of the mouth: ட ண ள, and ழ which doesn't touch). English t and d sit in between, on the gum ridge — so Tamils hear English t as ட!

To make a dental த, put your tongue firmly against the teeth — it sounds soft, almost like 'th'. To make a retroflex ட, curl the tongue tip up and back and flick it forward: it sounds hollow and heavy. Practise the pairs slowly.
tips: த: tongue tip visible between the teeth if you look in a mirror.
ட: tongue tip hidden, curled back; you feel the underside of the tongue touch the palate.
Between vowels ட becomes a quick flap — like a very short American 'r' with a d.

pronunciation.title: Word-final u and the extra vowels of speech
pronunciation.body:
Tamil words cannot end in a hard stop, so a huge number end in **-u**: வீடு, பத்து, பாட்டு. In normal speech this final u is often **not rounded**: it becomes a short, relaxed vowel like the 'i' in 'roses' (ɨ). It is still there — never drop it completely — but don't pronounce it like a clear 'oo'.

Spoken Tamil also **adds a -u** to words that end in a consonant in writing: பல் → பல்லு *pallu*, கண் → கண்ணு *kaṇṇu*, பால் → பாலு. And English loanwords get one too: 'bus' → பஸ்ஸு *bassu*, 'fan' → ஃபேனு. Hearing this extra vowel is key to understanding fast speech.
tips: Final -u: lips relaxed, not pushed forward.
When a suffix follows, the -u usually disappears: வீடு + -ல → வீட்டுல (the ட doubles).
Don't confuse the relaxed final u with a final i — பத்து vs பத்தி.

pronunciation.title: Written vs spoken: the contractions you will hear
pronunciation.body:
Spoken Tamil systematically shortens written forms. Learn these patterns and you can link what you read with what you hear:

• **-கிறேன் / -கிறது** (present tense) → **-றேன் / -து**: செய்கிறேன் → செய்யுறேன் *seyyurēn*.
• **இருக்கிறது** → **இருக்கு** *irukku*; **இல்லை** → **இல்ல** *illa*.
• **-கள்** (plural) → **-ங்க** *-nga* in pronouns and verbs: நீங்கள் → நீங்க, வாருங்கள் → வாங்க.
• **-இல்** (in) → **-ல** *-la*: வீட்டில் → வீட்டுல.
• **-ஐ** (object) and final **-ai** → *-a* or *-e*: அதை → அத *ada*; இலை → 'ile'.
• **ன்று** → **ண்ணு/ன்னு**: ஒன்று → ஒண்ணு *oṇṇu*; என்று → ன்னு *-nnu*.
• Final **-ம்** → nasalised vowel: மரம் ≈ *maraṃ*; வேண்டும் → வேணும் *vēṇum*.

None of these is 'slang' — they are how educated Tamils speak in every everyday situation.
tips: When reading spoken dialogue, sound it out — the spelling is close to speech.
Use spoken forms when talking; use written forms only for reading, signs and formal writing.
Spoken -ங்க (nīnga, vānga, sollunga) is your politeness marker — use it a lot.

pronunciation.title: Rhythm and question intonation
pronunciation.body:
Tamil has **no strong word stress**: syllables are fairly even, with a slight prominence on the first syllable of a word. Long vowels and doubled consonants, not stress, give a word its shape. Speaking English-style, with one loud syllable and swallowed others, makes Tamil hard to understand.

Yes/no questions are usually marked by the suffix **-ஆ** *-ā* on the word being asked about, with a **rising pitch** on that final ā: காபி வேணுமா? *kāpi vēṇumā?* 'Do you want coffee?'. The suffix **-ஓ** *-ō* adds doubt ('I wonder…'), and **-ஏ** *-ē* adds emphasis. Questions with a question word (என்ன, எங்க…) fall at the end like statements. Tamils also use a characteristic sideways **head wobble** to mean 'yes / OK / I'm listening'.
tips: Put the -ā on the word you are really asking about: நீங்களா? 'You?' vs போறீங்களா? 'Are you going?'.
Let pitch rise on the final ā of a yes/no question, and fall on question-word questions.
Keep syllables even — think 'machine gun', not 'Morse code'.
